ramie.origin: Ramie is the bast fiber of Boehmeria nivea, a perennial plant long known in trade as China grass, whose fiber lies in the stem bark. Ramie has been used for several millennia, and population genomic studies now detect domestication, improvement and feralization signatures in cultivated and wild forms. It is a niche fiber: a 2026 review puts 2018 output at about 100,000 tonnes, against about 310,000 tonnes of flax, although its production value exceeded that of hemp or flax. Much current breeding research comes from Chinese institutes, including the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences' Institute of Bast Fiber Crops.
ramie.structure: Once degummed, ramie is nearly pure cellulose, and its single fiber cells are exceptionally long, reported at about 20 to 250 mm, so it can be spun as individual cells rather than as bundles. Cellulose microfibrils lie very close to the fiber axis, with a microfibril angle of about 3 to 7.5 degrees, which gives high stiffness and dimensional stability but low extension, about 2.5% at break. Raw bast is heavily gummed: sun-dried fibers contain about 28.5% non-cellulosic matter, including about 14.7% hemicellulose, 5.1% pectin, 1.3% waxes and only about 1% lignin. The pectin is mainly low-esterified homogalacturonan with less branched rhamnogalacturonan I, in a ratio of about 1.7 to 1.
ramie.process: Stems are harvested and the bark is decorticated into ribbons that still carry most of their gums. Unlike jute and some other bast crops, ramie's pectin is difficult to remove effectively by natural retting, although it can be hydrolyzed by dilute acid or alkali, so ribbons are chemically degummed, typically by boiling in alkaline solutions, then washed and dried. Enzymatic degumming with pectate lyases from actinomycetes and other microbes has been studied since the 1990s; one crude enzyme preparation reduced residual gum to about 14.7% in 24 hours, and enzyme cocktails tailored to ramie pectin structure are being developed. The degummed fiber is then prepared for spinning, often in blends.
ramie.performance: Ramie is strong, stiff and lustrous and absorbs and releases moisture readily. The low microfibril angle that gives it strength also makes it inextensible, so fabrics wrinkle readily and feel crisp. Insufficiently degummed or untreated ramie yarns carry stiff protruding fiber ends that cause a pricking sensation on skin; cellulase or pectinase treatments soften the fiber and reduce this hairiness. It dyes with cellulose dye classes and chars rather than melts, and alkali treatment is used to modify ramie fabric for composites. Laboratory studies report bacteriostatic behavior of ramie fiber, but such findings apply to the tested material, not to every fabric.
ramie.identify: Burn tests are indicative only; ramie burns like other cellulose fibers, with a paper-like smell and soft ash. Microscopy shows long, thick-walled cells with a lumen, and the length of isolated cells, which can far exceed the roughly 17 to 25 mm of flax elementary fibers, is a useful clue. Its very low lignin distinguishes it from jute in staining tests. FTIR confirms cellulose but does not separate ramie from flax or hemp. Ramie blends are sometimes sold as linen-look fabrics, so the fiber content line matters.
ramie.labeling: Ramie is labeled by its fiber name and percentage by weight under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303 in the United States, and under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 in the EU. China grass is a common name, not a separate fiber, and ramie may not be described as linen or flax. Organic claims can be certified under standards such as GOTS where organic cultivation is documented. Degumming chemistry, a major environmental question for ramie, is not addressed by the fiber name.
ramie.past: Ramie belongs to the long East Asian tradition of bast-fiber cloth and has been cultivated for several millennia. Its modern history has been shaped by degumming: the fiber is strong and fine, but its gums resist retting and require chemical or enzymatic removal, which is costly and raises environmental concerns. From the 1990s researchers developed microbial pectinolytic enzymes to replace hot alkali, and in the past decade sequencing, genetic mapping and transformation work have aimed to breed varieties with lower pectin and hemicellulose. Newer research also tests ramie in biodegradable composites and even as a braided surgical suture.
